newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark unswayed by new Chinese rights pledge.
newsitem.headline: Denmark unswayed by new Chinese rights pledge.

text.p: Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said on Tuesday that Denmark would table a motion critising China's human rights record despite a new pledge from Beijing to sign an economic and social rights covenant.
Speaking at a news briefing he said that the Danish-led motion would shortly be tabled at a Geneva meeting of the U.N. Human Rights Commission.
"The decision to table the resolution has been taken. It will be tabled on Tuesday or Wednesday," he told reporters.
He did not reveal its exact wording but said that its "themes" included freedom of speech and assembly and the plight of political prisoners.
China said on Monday it would sign the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights but was silent on a similar pact on political freedoms.
Beijing would sign the covenant before the end of the year and was studying related domestic legislation, President Jiang Zemin told visiting French Defence Minister Charles Millon.
Petersen welcomed the Chinese pledge but said that such undertakings were not new.

"We have discussed the question of the U.N. conventions with the Chinese for years. It has been a constant theme in the conversations which I, and other EU foreign ministers have had over the years, that we have urged China to sign the two major conventions on political and social rights," he said.
"The Chinese have on several occasions raised the prospect that they would do so. I hope of course that China will do it now, it would be a great step forward," he added.
Denmark decided to table its censure alone after dissent within the European Union foiled plans for a joint EU motion.
It has since been joined as co-sponsor by the United States and Britain and Petersen said that between 10 and 12 other EU members intended to back the motion.
China has warned that Denmark faces political and economic repercussions if it goes ahead and Danish businesses with heavy investments in China have expressed their concern.

While Petersen enjoys overwhelming parliamentary support for his action, local newspapers are asking if little Denmark, with a population of five million, is biting off more than it can chew in the foreign policy arena.
They cite its offer to join peace efforts in Albania and a draft plan to offer a NATO security umbrella to the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, with Denmark as a major partner.

A cartoon on the front page of the Danish Berlingske Tidende daily on Tuesday showed a reluctant Petersen, in a Viking helmet and clutching a shield, being pushed toward a monstrous Chinese dragon by U.S. President Bill Clinton and British Premier John Major.
It is captioned, "St Niels and the Dragon."
